extracted.intended_audience: journalists, editors, newsroom managers, freelancers and media organisations interested in constructive/solutions journalism
extracted.subtask_description: A practice-oriented framework describing what constructive (solutions) journalism is and how to do it, centered on three elements (Focus on Solutions, Multiple Perspectives, Constructive Dialogue) with concrete sub-criteria for researching, producing and moderating news content.

rubrics_metrics.name: People-friendly journalism / common good focus
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructive journalism is people-friendly journalism – journalism that expressly puts the common good and the interests of people at its core.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also called 'user-friendly' in digital slang; applies to freelancers and major networks alike. The normative orientation is toward the common good and users' interests when deciding topics, tone and formats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand users' needs / user-centeredness
rubrics_metrics.description: To ensure journalism reaches its intended audience, journalists must understand users' needs: What is relevant to them? How would they like to be informed? And how can they communicate with us if they want to know more?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Particularly important in the digital age where journalism competes for attention. Implies continuous exchange about user needs, adapting formats and channels, community-building and communication built on equality and mutual respect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Future-oriented, fact-based, nuanced picture of reality
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructive journalism aims to give media users a future-oriented, fact-based, nuanced picture of reality by researching solutions as meticulously as problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counteracts a one-sided negative worldview and bolsters experiences of self-efficacy by illustrating potential courses of action. Emphasises accuracy, nuance and orientation toward possible futures rather than only describing problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on Solutions (element)
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructive journalism goes beyond identifying problems to reporting on solutions—researching how problems can be overcome and making the solutions core to the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The solutions approach should be the core of the story (not merely a closing paragraph). Central research question: 'Who is doing it better?' Use the Solutions Journalism Network criteria as a quality-control checklist to avoid greenwashing, activism or PR.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placing Possible Solutions Front and Center
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporting focuses on attempts to solve a problem and examining how they work; problems are also uncovered but reporting doesn't stop there.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The solutions-oriented piece should show how people can effectively deal with societal problems; the solutions approach is substantive and central rather than tokenistic or relegated to the end of the article.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence That Proves Effectiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigate attempts to solve a problem that have already been implemented and look for evidence that proves an approach is effective — not just good intentions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use empirical evidence: studies, surveys, evaluations. Effectiveness can also be documented qualitatively via interviews with people helped by the solution or with independent experts. This reduces risk of reporting unproven claims as solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transferability of an Approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess and report on a story's transferability: why a particular (possible) solution is newsworthy for others and what others can learn from it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask how exactly the approach works, what is required to apply it elsewhere, and to what extent local environment or context determines success. Emphasise practical lessons that can be learned and adapted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits and Hurdles
rubrics_metrics.description: Show the limits of possible solutions as critically as evidence of success; avoid presenting ideas as miracle cures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain when and why a solution may fail, what conditions are necessary, and which factors function versus which do not. Treat success as conditional and context-dependent rather than binary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple Perspectives (element)
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructive journalism consciously focuses on diversity and different perspectives to reflect the world in its complexity and counter oversimplification and polarization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This includes internal newsroom diversity and awareness of blind spots/biases. Relevance derives from addressing the information interests of many people in society rather than a single viewpoint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversity
rubrics_metrics.description: The breadth of perspectives in reporting is intrinsically tied to the diversity of staff; key markers include social, ethnic and geographical origins, religion, sexual identity and gender, family forms, education levels and place of residence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diverse staffing helps depict society comprehensively and reach diverse audiences (also an economic necessity). Public media have obligations to represent varied voices; practically, newsrooms should assess whether every voice is allowed to speak.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complexity
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporting that includes diverse perspectives counters oversimplification of complex situations into two opinions or poles and resists presenting false equivalencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use visualization, data, and systemic thinking: ask who is affected beyond the 'usual suspects' and avoid binary framings. Present shades of gray and multiple dimensions of an issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Angle and Zoom
rubrics_metrics.description: Broadening perspective by zooming out (wider angle) or zooming in (more detail) — adjusting time frames, geographic or societal foci to change the story's contours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: changing the temporal starting point of a story, reporting on-site vs. international comparisons, or choosing micro/meso/macro societal levels. Combining different angles and scales can produce richer reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-reflection
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists should reflect on how their reporting affects users and how their own cognitive biases and heuristics shape their view of reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise common cognitive distortions (e.g., confirmation bias) and work to mitigate them. The Bonn Institute links journalism with psychology to help reporters identify and compensate for habitual thinking patterns; absolute objectivity is acknowledged as unattainable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive Dialogue (element)
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists act as moderators of public dialogue, creating spaces for exchange, facilitating conversations across backgrounds and encouraging peaceful, future-oriented debate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constructive dialogue fosters social cohesion and improves discourse. It includes continuous exchange about user needs, reaching new audiences, and building community management based on equality and mutual respect. The Bonn Institute derives four criteria from mediation and communication psychology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Similarities, Not Differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructive dialogue focuses on similarities and possible solutions rather than statically referencing opposing positions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask what justified interests or needs underlie positions and what is acceptable to all sides; this approach opens perspectives and can reveal shared paths rather than entrenching polarization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empathic Interest
rubrics_metrics.description: The willingness to put oneself in another's shoes and seriously examine their position is essential for good discussion; active listening is central.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In interviews, panels or user conversations, active listening and follow-up questions show appreciation and foster understanding. Empathic interest supports meaningful exchange and helps moderators surface underlying concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omnipartiality
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt the mediator-like professional attitude of omnipartiality: be equally empathetic and attentive to all sides so everyone's concerns and expectations are heard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Particularly important for chronically unheard societal groups. Note limits: omnipartiality has boundaries when interlocutors violate democratic discourse rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forward-looking
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructive dialogue emphasizes future-oriented questioning — asking 'To what end?' and 'Where to?' rather than only 'Why?' and 'From where?'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use systematic questioning techniques (inspired by solution-focused therapy) to explore potential, next steps and constructive pathways rather than re-litigating problems alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid greenwashing, activism and PR
rubrics_metrics.description: Solutions-oriented reporting must avoid becoming uncritical advocacy, greenwashing or repackaged PR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the Solutions Journalism Network criteria (evidence, transferability, limits) as safeguards; critically assess claims, seek independent evaluation and guard against simply amplifying promotional narratives.
